title: Microsoft 365 Copilot And Power BI: The Easiest Way To Chat With Your Data
story_key: M365 Copilot integration with Power BI semantic models: GA
summary: Chris Webb argues that organisations already using Power BI and M365 Copilot should start their chat-with-data work by connecting the two, since the M365 Copilot and Cowork integration with Power BI semantic models is now generally available. He says it replaces the side-pane approach of Power BI Copilot, reuses existing semantic model work such as synonyms and AI instructions, and can combine Power BI data with Work IQ context. He also describes the cost model: querying needs only an M365 Business Premium licence plus capacity CUs for DAX queries, while Cowork credits may apply for complex tasks. The post is written by a Microsoft employee and is advice rather than independent evaluation.
why_it_matters: For a Fabric and Power BI shop with M365 Copilot licences, this is a GA path to natural-language access to existing semantic models that avoids the older Copilot capacity and AI cost model.

title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
story_key: Latent Space: Arca agent architecture for long-horizon financial work
summary: Latent Space interviewed Aman Singh, lead AI engineer at wealth manager Arca, about how the firm runs agents on multi-day client tasks. Agents do most background analysis and propose actions, while humans make final trading and money-movement decisions enforced by deterministic guardrails. Arca uses an internal memory system per client, its own model-routing harness (Claude is the primary provider, with a meta-agent that proposes harness changes from advisor feedback and traces), and sandboxed code execution with strict output formats before data reaches the backend.
why_it_matters: It shows concrete patterns for a production agent system with human approval gates, such as deterministic tool restrictions, owning the harness to stay portable across model providers, and using traces and feedback to improve the harness.

title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
story_key: Anthropic: FlashProve zkSNARK provable inference prototype
summary: Anthropic researchers present FlashProve, an open-source system based on zero-knowledge succinct proofs (zkSNARKs) that would let a model provider commit to a model and prove each response came from it, without revealing the weights. Their benchmark on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B mixture-of-experts model, 4-bit quantized) reports about 110 tokens/second per H100 GPU, roughly 19 MB of proof per 1,024-token request, and about 70-95x the GPU time of running the model on vLLM. They also release a fast C++ verifier and Lean formal proofs of the top-level security claims. The figures are the authors' own and not yet independently replicated, and they describe the work as intermediate progress.
why_it_matters: If you route LLM calls through third parties or need to verify which model served a response, this points to a future option, but at the current overhead it is a research prototype rather than something to adopt within months.

title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
story_key: Claude Platform: message threads public beta
summary: Anthropic has released message threads in public beta on the Claude Platform. With a thread, agents send only new messages and the previous response ID each turn instead of resending the full conversation, which the post says cuts time to first token for long sessions. The post reports a median TTFT drop of about 35% for requests of 500k to 1M tokens in Claude Code, where the feature is on by default for most users. Token usage stays the same because Claude still reads the full conversation each turn, and a thread expires 5 minutes after its last request.
why_it_matters: If I build long-running Claude agents, I can cut latency by threading requests instead of resending full histories, though I need to plan for the 5-minute expiry and the unchanged token cost.

title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
story_key: Transformers: Model Integration Contracts (transformers-mic)
summary: Hugging Face describes transformers-mic, a proposed standard for packaging small, CPU-runnable test fixtures (shrunk versions of real checkpoints) plus usage paths and reviewed baselines, so model integration bugs can be caught on PRs. They report that a small UMT5 fixture flagged a regression that let the decoder see future tokens, which sat in main for about two months and was missed by forward-pass-only tests. The post also covers the shrinking recipe, weight-initialization choices, and a CLI called tmic.
why_it_matters: If you integrate or customize open models with Transformers, this offers a cheap, CPU-based way to catch regressions on PRs that scheduled GPU suites miss, and a pattern you could adapt for your own LLM pipelines.

title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation
story_key: CoworkOS: general-purpose agent harness for long-horizon work
summary: A Renmin University team presents CoworkOS, an agent harness that separates task strategy (the model decides actions, delegation and acceptance) from execution management (the runtime keeps state and feedback). It adds subagents, shared editable workspaces and persistent memory for long-running work. The authors report competitiveness with Codex and DeepSeek Harness across 12 benchmarks, and a case study where automated post-training raised an average benchmark score from 33.19 to 42.95. The results are self-reported by one group and the paper has modest traction (69 upvotes).
exclusion_reason: low significance: single-group self-reported agent harness results with no independent replication; interesting architecture but not yet something to adopt

title: How to test AI agent skills and own your context
story_key: Tabular Editor: how to test AI agent skills with evals
summary: The article explains how to test whether an agent skill (reusable instructions loaded into an agent's context) actually helps, by re-running the same prompt with and without the skill, or with two skill versions, and comparing results over several runs. In the authors' test on a Tabular Editor CLI skill, the skill made Claude Opus 5 follow the steps and report issues it otherwise missed. It also argues that skills should be hand-written rather than generated by an agent, citing a study in which AI-generated skills performed worse than no skill, and reports that an AI-rewritten version of their skill contained factually wrong statements.
why_it_matters: If you build Claude-based workflows around Power BI or Fabric tooling, this gives a concrete, cheap method (ablation plus regression tests on saved prompts) to check that your skills earn their context cost and to avoid agent-written instructions.
